plain: Treat the seed's noise as a smooth continuous shape instead of searching move by move.
why: The noise really is one fixed function of the seed, so the world can be read as a shape. But the route still has to be searched on a graph, because crafting, mining and stamina are steps, not smooth motion.
keep: Read the world as a shape (islands, loops, sealed caves) to shrink the search, then still run an exact shortest-route search on the rules.
test: On a fixed seed set the solver finds the same cost as Dijkstra and uses fewer node expansions than the BFS baseline.

plain: Islands, loops and sealed caves can be computed straight from the seed in constant time.
why: Any single cell can be the one bridge that joins two islands, so an exact count has to look at every cell: it cannot be constant time. Formulas for noise only give averages, not the counts of one real world. Also a resource cluster and a floor island are different things.
keep: Compute exact counts by a single scan of the loaded area (about one visit per cell), cached per chunk, with islands = b0, loops = b1, sealed caves = b2.
test: Cells visited per scan grows in proportion to cells in the area (not flat), and the counts equal a brute-force flood fill on 100 seeds.

plain: Mining and opening doors cut the map so islands and loops drop, opening tunnels between regions.
why: Mining can merge two islands, but it can also add a new loop, create a new island, or fill in a hole, depending on the cells around it. Placing a block can split an island. So counts move in both directions.
keep: Surgery as an exact local update: each edit changes (b0, b1) by one named move decided by the neighbours, and merging tunnels between regions is the b0-down case.
test: After every random mine or place edit the fast update equals a full recount, and placing a block on a one-cell bridge raises b0 by one.

plain: Game rules like stamina, speed caps and friction form a distance rule, and the best route is the shortest path under it.
why: A shortest path under a cost rule is real. But the game is made of steps, stamina depends on history so cost is not a function of position alone, and friction is not something a metric can describe. The smooth geodesic equation does not apply to a grid.
keep: Use the cost rule as edge weights on a graph of position plus inventory plus stamina, and find the best route with Dijkstra or A-star; treat the geodesic as the fine-grid limit.
test: The solver's route cost equals Dijkstra on the full state graph and equals the simulator's tick count on a world where crafting first is faster.

plain: Fixed-point theorems find the best strategy for several players without searching game moves.
why: Fixed-point theorems prove an equilibrium exists but give no way to compute it, and finding one is hard in general. A speedrun of a seeded world has one player, where the best play is just the shortest route.
keep: Drop it from sealrun's single-player any% run. If a two-sided game ever appears, use the zero-sum minimax value (an exact method already in monodromy).
test: The toy any% has exactly one agent and its optimum equals the Dijkstra route; a future zero-sum case checks the minimax value against a linear-program answer.

plain: Flatten twisted dungeons with conformal maps, and predict unseen parts of the world by analytic continuation.
why: Conformal maps keep angles, not walking distances, and a block dungeon is not a smooth complex shape. Hashed noise is not analytic, so unseen parts cannot be guessed from seen parts.
keep: No guessing is needed: the seed gives the unseen chunk exactly by running the generator for it, and that exactness is testable.
test: A chunk generated alone is byte-identical to the same chunk generated inside a larger area, for 100 seeds.

plain: Lyapunov exponents and coherent structures from chaos theory find stable routes through chaotic fights and physics.
why: These tools are real for smooth moving systems and tell where tiny changes blow up. The toy game is a discrete rules machine with no chaos, so there is nothing for them to measure there.
keep: Keep as a later robustness check for games with real physics: avoid routes that pass through high-sensitivity places. Port the exponent code from monodromy then, not now.
test: The ported exponent code reproduces the known values for the Henon and Lorenz systems from monodromy before it is applied to any game.

plain: Embedding noise in complex numbers or quaternions lets a hidden phase rotate through fractal steps instantly.
why: Adding an imaginary part adds no information, because we would be inventing it. Fractal escape times have no shortcut formula: they are computed by iterating. Perlin noise is not an iterated map in the first place.
keep: Retire it. Use integer hash noise with fixed-point gradients, which already gives a byte-identical world with no complex numbers.
test: The world generator passes the fixed-fingerprint test on 100 seeds using integer arithmetic only.

plain: The fractal dimension of each Betti slice summarises an infinitely complex world in constant time.
why: A finite grid has no true fractal dimension; only a slope fitted over several sizes, with noise (monodromy measures about 2.7 percent spread across seeds), and it needs a pass over the data. Only the degree-0 estimator has a theorem behind it.
keep: Report a fractal-dimension estimate per loaded region, labelled as an estimate with its spread, computed from monodromy's tree-based method on cluster points.
test: The estimator returns the right dimension within a stated tolerance on uniform random points in 2D, before it is used on any world.

plain: Benchmark the seed-to-route solver against a Monte Carlo tree search baseline on Crafter or custom seeded grids.
why: This is a testable plan. It only means something if the rival gets the same seeds and budget and can reach the optimum when given plenty of time. Crafter has random creatures and no Rust port, so it is not a fixed-seed fair test.
keep: Benchmark on custom deterministic seed grids in in-game ticks, and add a fair-rival guard. Crafter is deferred.
test: On a fixed seed set the solver's ticks are lower than the baseline's at equal budget, and the baseline with a huge budget matches the true optimum.
